name: Centimorgan to Percentage Calculator
seoTitle: Centimorgan to Percentage Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: A centimorgan is one unit of genetic distance: a 1% chance of recombination between two loci per generation. Free centimorgan to percentage calculator: enter
summary:
A centimorgan is one unit of genetic distance: a 1% chance of recombination between two loci per generation. It returns recombination frequency (simple), recombination frequency (Haldane), recombination frequency (Kosambi) and cM for 10% recombination, and the panel shows all of them at once.

Over short distances the map distance in cM and the recombination percentage are the same number; over long ones they diverge, and this calculator applies the mapping functions that account for it. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: How do I use the Centimorgan to Percentage?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: map distance of 20 cM.

Substituting them into the formula gives recombination frequency (simple) of 20%, recombination frequency (haldane) of 16.48%, recombination frequency (kosambi) of 19%, cm for 10% recombination of 0.1014 cM.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Above about 10 cM the simple 1:1 correspondence breaks down because double crossovers restore the parental configuration and are not counted.

  • Haldane's function assumes crossovers occur at random (no interference); Kosambi's assumes interference and converts a given cM to a smaller recombination percentage.

  • The maximum observable recombination frequency is 50%, which corresponds to independent assortment however far apart the loci are.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Treating cM as a physical distance in base pairs — one cM is about a megabase in humans on average, but it varies tenfold.
  • Adding recombination percentages directly across a long interval.

faq.a: Only at small distances; at 20 cM the recombination frequency is closer to 18% under Haldane's model.

faq.q: Why does recombination top out at 50%?
faq.a: Because past that point linked loci are indistinguishable from unlinked ones.

faq.q: What does the Centimorgan to Percentage actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns recombination frequency (simple), recombination frequency (Haldane), recombination frequency (Kosambi) and cM for 10% recombination. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
